records.sourceFile: The Relationships Between Reaction Time Scores and False Start Penalties of Offensive Linemen in the National Football League (NFL).pdf

paper.citation: Bowman JK, Krywaruczenko D, De Flon BG, Boone RT. The Relationships Between Reaction Time Scores and False Start Penalties of Offensive Linemen in the National Football League (NFL). Perceptual and Motor Skills. 2024.
paper.abstract: The study examined whether the Athletic Intelligence Quotient (AIQ) reaction time measures relate to false start penalties per game in NFL offensive linemen. Archival data from 85 linemen tested before the draft in 2014 to 2021 were analysed with ANOVA, correlations and hierarchical regression, controlling for draft pick and position. Higher accuracy on the choice reaction time task accounted for a statistically significant share of the variance in false starts per game beyond draft pick and position. The authors discuss the practical value of such cognitive assessments for player development.
paper.tldr: In NFL offensive linemen, lower accuracy on a choice reaction time test was linked to more false start penalties per game, even after accounting for draft position and position played. The link is modest and based on one penalty type, so it is a reason for targeted development work rather than a selection rule.
paper.methods: Archival analysis of 85 NFL offensive linemen (centers excluded) who completed the AIQ before the draft between 2014 and 2021 and played at least 17 games by the end of 2021. The outcome was false starts per game. Predictors were simple reaction time commission errors and choice reaction time d-prime. Analyses were a one-way ANOVA by position, zero-order correlations and hierarchical regression, entering draft pick, position, then the two reaction time measures. Only anonymised archival data were used.
paper.findings: Tackles averaged 0.16 false starts per game, guards 0.10 and players who played both positions 0.12 (F(2,84) = 3.96, p = .02). Simple reaction time commission errors (r = .22) and choice reaction time d-prime (r = .29) were correlated with false starts per game (p < .05). Draft pick round was the first significant predictor (beta = .31). After draft pick and position were entered, the two reaction time measures added about 6% explained variance (delta F(2,76) = 3.00, p = .05). Choice reaction time d-prime was the only unique predictor (beta = .23), and the full model explained 21% of the variance (F(5,76) = 3.91, p = .003).
paper.limitations: Small sample from one test battery, and the power analysis gave 80% power only for large effects, while the observed correlations were small (r = .22 to .29) and the added variance step sat at p = .05. Table 1 uses N = 82 while the text reports 85 linemen, Table 2 omits several coefficients, and Table 1 shows the choice reaction time correlation without a minus sign although the text describes a negative association. Centers were excluded, false starts are a narrow measure of line play, and scheme, coaching and opponent factors were not measured. The lead author is listed as Chief Science Officer of Athletic Intelligence Measures, LLC, although the article declares no conflicts of interest.
paper.practicalImplications: For linemen who score low on choice reaction accuracy, coaches could consider extra practice on counts and cadences and drills with noise or simulated distraction, as the authors suggest. These ideas were not tested in this study, so they should be treated as hypotheses. Staff can track false starts as a simple game indicator alongside the test score.
paper.athleteDev: In this sample, lower choice reaction time accuracy was linked to more false start penalties beyond draft position. It can inform planning of vigilance and count-based work, but the study does not show that such training reduces false starts.
paper.rtp: The study looks at penalties in healthy players during games and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to play, so it cannot be used for return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: The effect of exercise-induced fatigue and heat exposure on soccer-specific decision-making during high intensity intermittent exercise.pdf

paper.citation: Donnan KJ, Williams EL, Stanger N. The effect of exercise-induced fatigue and heat exposure on soccer-specific decision-making during high-intensity intermittent exercise. PLoS ONE. 2022;17(12):e0279109.
paper.abstract: Nine well-trained male soccer players completed a 92-minute cycling intermittent sprint protocol at 32 C (hot) and 18 C (temperate), responding to soccer-specific decision-making trials throughout. Physical output, decision-making, appraisal, affect and plasma metanephrines were measured.
paper.tldr: In nine trained soccer players, heat lowered soccer-specific decision-making during a prolonged intermittent sprint protocol. Power output also fell in the second half only in the heat, with a more threatening appraisal and higher stress hormone levels.
paper.methods: Laboratory study with nine well-trained male soccer players, planned as a counterbalanced design for 10 players but stopped early because of the pandemic (five players began in 32 C, four in 18 C). Participants completed a 92-minute cycling intermittent sprint protocol (5-s sprints against 8% body mass with active recovery at 35% of the VO2peak from an incremental test) at 32 C and 50% relative humidity or 18 C and 50% relative humidity. Soccer-specific decision-making was scored against expert panel responses and verbal think-aloud reports were coded. Analysis used two-way repeated-measures ANOVA and content analysis.
paper.findings: Decision-making scores were lower in 32 C than 18 C (86.87 +/- 7.95% vs 92.49 +/- 3.13%, main effect p = 0.030), but there was no condition by time interaction. Peak power fell in the second half of the protocol only in the heat (about 7%), with no significant between-condition difference in either half. Plasma normetanephrine was higher in the heat at half-time (p = 0.012) and post-exercise (p < 0.001), and metanephrine was higher post-exercise (p = 0.006 to 0.009). Players verbalised less future planning in the heat (p = 0.030, d = 0.20), and threat appraisal and unpleasant affect were higher in the heat (p = 0.007 and p = 0.008).
paper.limitations: Only nine players were analysed, and the planned 10 were not reached. Trial order was only partly counterbalanced. A cycling protocol was used, which the authors say may produce less physiological strain than running. The decision-making task was visual only and did not reproduce dual-task demands of match play. Decision-making was lower in the heat at all time points, including pre-exercise in the chamber, so passive heat exposure may explain part of the effect. Laboratory motivation may differ from matches. The think-aloud findings need caution given the number of analyses run. Core temperature averaged about 38.4 C in the heat, with no main condition effect, and the authors say this is lower than typical team-sport values.
paper.practicalImplications: In hot conditions, soccer players may make poorer decisions and lose work output, even when core temperature stays below common cut-offs. Staff planning training or matches in heat should consider decision-making as well as physical output. Players also reported more threat and unpleasant feelings in the heat, and the authors suggest strategies such as acclimatisation or re-appraisal could be considered.
paper.athleteDev: Heat can lower decision-making and second-half work output during intermittent exercise, even when core temperature stays around 38.4 C. Staff should consider cognitive as well as physical demands when preparing players for hot conditions.
paper.rtp: This study cannot be used for return-to-play decisions. It tested healthy trained players in a laboratory cycling protocol and includes no injury or rehabilitation outcomes.

records.sourceFile: The effects of mobile phone dependence on athletic performance and its mechanisms.pdf

paper.citation: Mei Z, Zhang Y, Fan Q, Luo S, Luo S. The effects of mobile phone dependence on athletic performance and its mechanisms. Frontiers in Psychology. 2024;15:1391258.
paper.abstract: Reviews how mobile phone dependence affects athletes' performance through individual and environmental factors, proposes neurobiological mechanisms centred on the brain reward system, and discusses the social cognitive model of self-regulation and the integrative model of self-control as explanatory frameworks.
paper.tldr: Mobile phone dependence in athletes is linked to disrupted sleep, mental fatigue, poorer decision-making and weaker coach relationships. Coaches could monitor phone use and build self-regulation and self-control skills, but the mechanisms still need testing.
paper.methods: Narrative review of previous studies on individual factors, environmental factors, neurobiological mechanisms and theoretical models of MPD and athletic performance. No search strategy is reported.
paper.findings: Stress and weak self-control may drive heavy phone use, and phone use can impair attention and decision-making. In a volleyball trial, social-media use before training blocked the decision-making improvement seen in controls, and in an eight-week swimming trial, 30 minutes of smartphone use before training increased mental fatigue and internal training load and inhibited 100-m and 400-m performance gains. The review proposes that phone reward cues act on the brain reward system and that microwave radiation may affect dopaminergic circuits, but it cites no athlete studies that test these links.
paper.limitations: No search method is reported. The authors note that causal links between MPD and performance are hard to establish because longitudinal studies are rare, and that the influence pathways and mechanisms need further investigation.
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches could limit phone and social-media use before training, and support athletes in building self-regulation and attention-control skills such as mindfulness. Athletes under stress may need extra attention for signs of problematic phone use.
paper.athleteDev: Phone use before training may reduce focus, decision-making and training gains. The authors suggest athletes avoid social media for at least two hours before sessions, but the review proposes this and does not test it.
paper.rtp: The review does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.
